summary: Defines an IPv6 unicast address format that is globally unique but intended for local communications, usually within a site. These addresses are not expected to be routable on the global Internet. It is a standards-track document.

plainLanguage.summary: Unique Local IPv6 addresses give a site an address prefix for internal communication that does not depend on an Internet provider. Their randomly generated identifier makes collisions between sites unlikely, but the addresses are meant to stay off the global Internet.

subtitle: Defines IPv6 addresses for local communication with prefixes designed to avoid site conflicts.

tldr.problem: Organizations need IPv6 addresses for internal use that do not depend on an Internet provider and are unlikely to conflict when sites connect.
tldr.mechanism: Unique Local Addresses use a known prefix and a pseudo-randomly generated global identifier to create a locally routed IPv6 prefix.
tldr.outcome: Sites can use these addresses for internal networks or private inter-site links, but they are not intended for global Internet routing and do not provide security by themselves.

today: RFC 4193 is a Proposed Standard defining Unique Local IPv6 Unicast Addresses and has no later replacement listed in this unit's metadata.

sections.title: IPv6 Addresses for Local Networks
sections.content:
Unique Local IPv6 Unicast Addresses are designed for communication inside a site and between a limited set of sites. They are not expected to be routed across the global Internet.

The known prefix makes the addresses easy to filter at site boundaries, while the locally generated identifier makes it unlikely that two organizations will use the same prefix. This can help sites merge or connect through a VPN without renumbering.
sections.plainLanguage: These addresses are for private IPv6 communication within a site or a connected set of sites. They are designed so that connecting two organizations is unlikely to create an address conflict.

sections.title: The Unique Local Address Format
sections.content:
The format begins with the FC00::/7 prefix, followed by an L bit, a 40-bit Global ID, a 16-bit Subnet ID, and a 64-bit Interface ID. The L bit is set for locally assigned identifiers in this specification.

The Global ID identifies the site's locally allocated prefix, the Subnet ID identifies a subnet within the site, and the Interface ID identifies an interface. The address is still an IPv6 unicast address and uses ordinary routing behavior inside its permitted scope.
sections.plainLanguage: The address contains a shared local prefix, a site identifier, a subnet identifier, and an interface identifier. Routers can handle it like other IPv6 unicast traffic within the site's routing domain.

sections.title: Generating a Global ID
sections.content:
A locally assigned Global ID must be generated pseudo-randomly and must not be chosen sequentially or from a well-known value. Random allocation makes independently created prefixes highly likely to differ.

The RFC gives a suggested algorithm that combines the current time with a system-specific identifier, computes a SHA-1 digest, and uses its least significant 40 bits as the Global ID. The ID is not mathematically guaranteed to be unique, but the specified probability of collision is very small for the expected scale.
sections.plainLanguage: Each site generates its identifier using a pseudo-random method rather than choosing it from a shared list. This makes two sites much less likely to choose the same local prefix.

sections.title: Keeping Local Addresses Local
sections.content:
Routers can carry these prefixes inside a site like other unicast routes. By default, exterior routing should neither advertise nor accept the full local-address block; operators may configure specific routes for inter-site communication.

Border routers and firewalls should block packets with local source or destination addresses from leaving the site unless an explicit route permits them. This limits accidental leakage and reflects that these prefixes are not designed for global route aggregation.
sections.plainLanguage: Local addresses can be routed within a site, and selected routes can connect private sites. Border routers should filter them by default so they do not become global Internet routes.

sections.title: DNS, VPNs, and Security
sections.content:
The RFC does not recommend placing locally assigned addresses in the global DNS, and reverse lookups for them must not be sent to global DNS servers. Sites can instead use local naming systems for local-only devices.

Unique Local addresses can support inter-site VPNs when appropriate routes are configured. They do not provide security by themselves; filters can limit where packets travel, while cryptographic protection must come from separate mechanisms.
sections.plainLanguage: Keep local address records in local naming systems so outside DNS does not receive queries for them. The addresses can work over configured VPN routes, but they do not encrypt traffic or authenticate a sender.
